The Torah Teaching and Public Work of Ḥakham Menahem Manasseh: A Historiographic, Ideational, and Structural Analysis of the Author of "Ahavat Ḥayyim"

This survey presents the life and teachings of Ḥakham Menahem Manasseh, an exemplary figure who constituted a spiritual bridge between the tradition of Turkish Jewry and the renewed Torah center in the Land of Israel. The text portrays him as a hidden righteous man who combined contradictions, who labored as a blacksmith for his livelihood by day and delved into Kabbalah by night, while establishing the "Ahavat Ḥayyim" society for charitable and educational enterprises. A central component of the essay is an analysis of his popular book *Ahavat Ḥayyim* (Love of Life), which makes homiletics, halakha, and moral tales accessible in clear language to the general public, and reflects his ethical teaching emphasizing love of Israel and concern for the needy. Ultimately, the source seeks to immortalize a leader who dedicated his life to spiritual and social repair, and whose legacy continues to pulse today in educational institutions and in his literary works.

The Torah Teaching and Public Work of Ḥakham Menahem Manasseh: A Historiographic, Ideational, and Structural Analysis of the Author of "Ahavat Ḥayyim"

The spiritual history of the Jewish settlement in the Land of Israel in the twentieth century is characterized by a dramatic transition between the old traditional world, as crystallized in the communities of the Ottoman Empire and the East, and the construction of a new Torah center responding to the challenges of modernity, Zionism, and the establishment of the State. At the heart of this process stands the multidimensional figure of Ḥakham Menahem Manasseh of blessed memory (1892–1968), a figure who combines within himself apparent contradictions: a kabbalistic sage hidden from all eyes who works as a simple laborer for his livelihood, and an activist public leader who founds charitable organizations and Torah institutions; a prolific author who composes a classic work of broad scope, and a man of toil who walks the alleyways of Jerusalem to collect penny by penny for orphans.[1, 2, 3] Analysis of his work reveals a spiritual influence constituting a bridge between generations and between cultures, which left an indelible mark on the Jewish bookshelf and on the social structure of the Sephardic community in Jerusalem and beyond.[2, 4]

The Roots in Turkey: Formation of the Torah Personality in the Shadow of the "Holy Grandfather"

The figure of Ḥakham Menahem Manasseh emerged from the rich spiritual soil of Turkish Jewry at the end of its golden age. He was born in the year 5653 (1892) in the village of Kayık near the city of Bursa, a place where ancient traditions of the sages of Sepharad were preserved.[3] His family was steeped in fear of Heaven, with his father, Ḥakham Ya'akov Manasseh, serving as his first guide in Torah and moral qualities. Nevertheless, his childhood years were fraught with difficulties; at only ten years old he was orphaned of his father, an event that shaped his deep sensitivity to orphans and widows that would accompany him throughout his adult life.[2, 3]

Following his father's death, young Menahem moved to the great spiritual center in Istanbul. There, despite his poverty and orphanhood, he integrated into the city's yeshivot and gained recognition from the great sages. The most significant encounter in those years was with the "Holy Grandfather," Rabbi Shelomo Eli'ezer Alfandari, who is considered one of the greatest of the generation in recent generations.[2, 3] Alfandari, who was known for his asceticism and his rigor in halakhic matters, identified in Menahem Manasseh the spiritual potential latent within him and became for him a model of the combination of Torah genius with piety and self-mortification.[3] In the year 5671 (1911) he married Esther Ḥarez, a righteous woman who stood by his side throughout all the tribulations of his life, and together they began to build their home on the foundations of the rootedness of Sephardic tradition.[2]

The Crucible: His Service in the Ottoman Army and Its Implications

The outbreak of the First World War interrupted the routine of Ḥakham Menahem's life. In the year 5673 (1913) he was forcibly conscripted into the Ottoman army, service that continued throughout the war years and subjected his faith to the most severe tests.[2, 3] Military service under field conditions, in an enemy state conducting bloody battles, required Menahem Manasseh to develop strategies of spiritual survival. He would study Torah at night inside the military tents, hiding a small candle so as not to be discovered by the officers.[3] Evidence of this can be found in stories about how he would smuggle wine for kiddush and kosher bread, while risking severe physical punishment. In one instance he was caught by an officer and beaten cruelly, but even then he did not retreat from his devotion to the commandments.[3]

This experience in the Ottoman army was not merely a period of suffering, but a formative stage in his approach to "love of Israel." There, among the simple Jewish soldiers, Ḥakham Menahem saw the thirst for the word of God and the need for spiritual strengthening in times of crisis. In those years he made his famous vow: if he merited to survive the inferno, he would ascend to the Land of Israel and dedicate his life to spreading Torah and helping the needy in Zion.[2] His survival from the war was perceived by him as an open miracle obligating him to complete devotion to his public mission.

Settlement in Jerusalem: Blacksmith by Day and Kabbalist by Night

The immigration to the Land of Israel, which occurred between the years 1915 and 1918 (5675–5678), marked the beginning of the Jerusalem chapter of his life.[2, 3] Ḥakham Menahem chose to settle in the Beit Yisra'el neighborhood, a neighborhood known for its population of scholars and laborers. His choice of a way of life of "hidden piety" was conscious and intentional. In order not to derive benefit from the crown of Torah and in order to maintain anonymity that would enable him to engage in Kabbalah and spiritual repairs without attracting attention, he worked for his livelihood as a blacksmith.[1, 5]

The blacksmith's work, which was hard and dirty physical labor, served him as a kind of mask. During the day he appeared as a simple laborer providing for his family's sustenance, but with nightfall and until dawn, he became one of the pillars of the Jerusalem kabbalistic world.[3, 4] This combination of "Torah and labor" in its Sephardic-kabbalistic version placed him in line with other hidden sages in the Jerusalem of that period, who saw in manual labor a religious value guaranteeing purity of intentions.[4]

The Torah Network: Rabbi Peti'ah and Rabbi Alpiyyah

In Jerusalem Ḥakham Menahem became an inseparable part of an inner circle of kabbalists. He connected with the kabbalist Rabbi Yitsḥak Alpiyyah and became his close disciple.[1] The relationship between the two deepened when Ḥakham Menahem integrated into the spiritual repairs and speech fasts that Rabbi Alpiyyah organized, and drew from him knowledge in esoteric Torah.[1, 6]

With the immigration of the renowned Babylonian kabbalist, Rabbi Yehudah Peti'ah, to Jerusalem in the year 5694 (1934), Ḥakham Menahem found in him another rabbi and guide. He became Rabbi Peti'ah's right hand, and assisted him in editing spiritual repairs for souls, writing amulets according to Kabbalah, and organizing mass prayers.[1] These august figures saw in Ḥakham Menahem Manasseh a figure of a "righteous man who is the foundation of the world." Rabbi Mordekhay Shar'abi, who was revered by the entire Jerusalem public, testified about him that he was among the thirty-six hidden righteous men of the generation, and even noted that he saw a "pillar of fire" above his head during his prayer.[4, 7]

The "Ahavat Ḥayyim Society": The Institution and the Vision

In the year 5690 (1930) Ḥakham Menahem decided to transform his informal activity into an institutionalized organization, and thus the "Ahavat Ḥayyim Society" was established.[1, 5] The name "Ahavat Ḥayyim" was not chosen by chance; it reflected his conception that the Torah is a "Torah of life" based on love—love of God, love of Torah, and love of Israel.

Spiritual Dissemination and Speech Fasts

The society set itself the goal of disseminating Torah among the general public, especially among those who could not dedicate all their time to study in yeshivot. Ḥakham Menahem established daily Torah classes in simple and accessible language, with emphasis on ethics and practical halakha.[1, 5] One of the central and unique activities of the society was organizing mass speech fasts, especially during the "Shovavim" days (weeks of the portions from Exodus to Mishpatim).[1, 8] He believed that the power of silence and concentration on study and prayer for an entire day could nullify harsh decrees against the people of Israel.

During the Second World War, when the Nazi threat reached the gates of the Land of Israel, the "Ahavat Ḥayyim Society" became a center of outcry and prayer. Ḥakham Menahem organized special repairs
and prayers at the graves of righteous individuals for the sake of peace for the inhabitants of the land and the end of the war.[1] His conception was that intensive spiritual activity on the hidden plane is the key to physical salvation on the revealed plane.

Charitable Works and "Giving in Secret"

Alongside spiritual activity, "Ḥevrat Ahavat Ḥayim" served as a community welfare center. Ḥakham Menaḥem was known for his extraordinary charity, as he himself would collect funds and distribute them to those in need in ways of "giving in secret" so as not to shame the recipients.[1, 2] He cared especially for widows and orphans, remembering his own orphanhood in Turkey. One of his practices was to visit poor families on Sabbath and festival eves and leave baskets of food by their door without their knowing who the donor was.[4]

Evidence of his devotion can be found in the story about raising funds for the wedding of an orphaned groom. The sages of Yeshivat Porat Yosef, who recognized his abilities and generous heart, charged him with obtaining the enormous sum of five hundred lira—a sum that was fantastical for a simple metalworker. Ḥakham Menaḥem did not shrink back, traveled to Tel Aviv and approached benefactors, while insisting on absolute truth in every single word that issued from his mouth, until he obtained the full amount.[4]

The Struggle for the Education of Immigrant Children

With the establishment of the State and the great waves of immigration from Eastern countries, Ḥakham Menaḥem identified a great spiritual danger. Many immigrant children were sent to educational frameworks that did not accord with the spirit of traditional Israel, and many families were compelled to send their children to work due to a difficult economic situation.[2, 4] Ḥakham Menaḥem acted decisively to change the situation. He hired teachers and study places at the expense of "Ḥevrat Ahavat Ḥayim," and provided food for the children so that their parents would agree to send them to study Torah instead of working.[2, 3]

In this activity Ḥakham Menaḥem was a partner in founding the organization "Yad la-Aḥim" (the activists), an organization intended to prevent foreign religious proselytizing and to return children to Torah education.[3, 4] He saw the struggle for the souls of children as the most urgent mission of the generation, and invested in it all his energy and money, sometimes at the expense of his most basic needs.[3]

The Monumental Work: The Book "Ahavat Ḥayim"

The most significant contribution of Ḥakham Menaḥem Menashe to the Jewish bookshelf is the book "Ahavat Ḥayim" on the Torah, which was first published in the year 5696 (1936).[1, 5, 9] The book quickly became a bestseller among Sephardic Jewry and Eastern communities, and it is found to this day in nearly every Jewish home that preserves the tradition of its forefathers.[5, 10]

Structure and Sources

The book "Ahavat Ḥayim" is structured according to the order of the weekly Torah portions, and each portion is divided into several layers that grant the reader a holistic study experience:

Homilies and Aggadot: Explications on the verses of the portion based on the Sages, the Midrashim, and the holy Zohar. Ḥakham Menaḥem used simple and clear language ("language accessible to every soul") in order to make profound ideas accessible.[3, 5]

Practical Halakhah: In each portion are integrated practical halakhot relevant to that period of the year or to issues arising from the portion. The halakhot were written according to the custom of the holy community of Sephardim and Eastern communities, relying on the "Beit Yosef," the "Kaf ha-Ḥayim," and early and late decisors.[5, 9, 11]

Stories and Parables: One of the unique characteristics of the book is the wealth of stories and tales. Ḥakham Menaḥem collected tales from rare manuscripts of Sephardic sages, including passages from the book "Me'am Lo'ez" that had not yet appeared in Hebrew at that time.[5, 9] The stories were intended to arouse the imagination and strengthen the personal morality of the student.

The Impact and Popularity

The book "Ahavat Ḥayim" filled a spiritual vacuum among the Sephardic public in the Land of Israel and in the diaspora. It served as a central educational tool for "householders"—working people who sought a concentrated study source for the Sabbath table, combining Torah and halakhah together with stories that also captivated the children.[3, 10] The new editions of the book, vocalized and printed in eye-pleasing letters, continue to appear and demonstrate the eternal relevance of his composition.[11]

His Philosophical Teaching: Foundations of Hope and Responsibility

Behind the deeds and books stood a consolidated philosophical teaching, whose roots are planted in the Kabbalah of the Ari and the Rashash, but whose fruits are intended for the common person in the market lanes.

Redemption from within Darkness: The Evening Prayer as Metaphor

Ḥakham Menaḥem developed a profound insight regarding the concept of redemption. He explained that specifically Jacob our forefather, the chosen of the patriarchs whose life was fraught with suffering and exile, instituted the evening prayer—a prayer recited at night.[2] According to Ḥakham Menaḥem, the night symbolizes the hour of judgment and the darkness of exile. The fact that a Jew prays at night teaches of "a light of hope" that never goes out. He expounded that specifically in the most difficult moments of the nation and of the individual, one must remember the covenant with God who will redeem us "from the hand of kings" and "from the grasp of all tyrants."[2]

The Severity of Publicly Shaming

A central theme in his ethical teaching was caution regarding respect for others. He warned sharply against publicly shaming, and claimed that publicly shaming is considered actual murder.[2] Ḥakham Menaḥem criticized those who pose as "righteous and zealots" who humiliate people who sinned publicly. He brought proof from the laws of the guilt-offering, which was burned at night so as not to shame the penitent.[2] For him, "love of Israel" was not a slogan, but a stringent halakhic and metaphysical demand: every Jew is a part of the Shekhinah, and harming him is harming the Creator Himself.

Charity as Cosmic Repair

Ḥakham Menaḥem saw the act of charity as an action of "unifying the Holy One, Blessed be He, and His Shekhinah." He explained that charity is not merely social assistance, but a spiritual force capable of raising the Shekhinah from the dust ("to raise the Shekhinah from the dust").[2] He emphasized that charity must be given for worthy purposes—to modest righteous individuals who hide their poverty, to orphans and to widows—and thereby the student and the donor become partners in the act of Creation and in the repair of the four worlds.[2]

Personal Practices and Ascetic Lifestyle

Despite his extensive public activity, Ḥakham Menaḥem maintained a lifestyle of extreme asceticism. He and his fellowship ("Ḥevrat Ahavat Ḥayim") practiced mortifications intended to atone for the sins of the generation. Testimonies tell of "rectifications of reincarnations" that included immersion in frozen mikva'ot in which blocks of ice had been placed, all this while engaging in complex kabbalistic intentions and unifications.[3]

His daily schedule was a model of time utilization:

Midnight: Rising to perform "Tikkun Ḥatzot" in weeping and supplication over the exile and the destruction.[3]

Dawn: Study of esoteric Torah and writing novellae in his books.[3]

Morning: Morning prayer at sunrise, followed by going out to metalworking labor for household sustenance.[1, 3]

Noon and Afternoon: Work in the workshop, while insisting on reciting Psalms and Mishnayot by heart.

Evening: Giving Torah lessons in the synagogue, receiving the public for counsel and blessing, and raising funds for charity.[3, 5]

He was very careful about guarding his tongue, and practiced fasts of speech not only during the days of "Shovavim" but whenever he felt there was a need for spiritual strengthening.[8, 12] His simplicity was so great that many of the people for whom he repaired metal utensils in his workshop did not know at all that he was one of the great kabbalists of Jerusalem.[3, 4]

His Death and Funeral: Secrets Revealed

Ḥakham Menaḥem Menashe passed away on the 12th of Elul 5728 (1968).[1, 2, 3] Toward the end of his life, he revealed to one of his sons that he had taken upon himself to go as atonement for the people of Israel in order to annul a harsh decree that hovered over the community.[4] He foresaw the exact date of his death and left detailed instructions regarding his funeral: he requested not to be carried on an ambulance or vehicle, but that his bier be carried by hand by means of "iron rods" alone, as was practiced in the Old City of Jerusalem.[3]

During his funeral, which was saturated with the tears of masses of Jerusalemites from all circles, many stories were revealed about miracles and salvations he had wrought in secret. Great rabbis, foremost among them Rabbi Mordekhai Share'abi and Rabbi Ovadiah Yosef, eulogized him and emphasized the loss of the "pillar of prayer" of the g
He is interred in the Sephardic section of Har HaMenuchot in Jerusalem, and his grave has become a lodestone for prayer and supplication.

The Continuity of the Legacy: The "Ahavat Chaim" Institutions Today

The legacy of Hakham Menahem Manasseh does not reside solely between the pages of his books, but thrives in the educational and charitable institutions established in his name and spirit.

Yeshivat Ahavat Chaim - Kokhav HaShachar

One of the prominent educational enterprises is Yeshivat "Ahavat Chaim," established in 5755 (1995) in the settlement of Kokhav HaShachar. The yeshiva was founded by a group of parents who sought to implement Hakham Menahem's conception: to see in every soul an "unpolished diamond." The yeshiva combines Torah study with manual labor (carpentry, metalwork, silversmithing), thereby continuing the path of Hakham Menahem, who combined tinsmithing with supreme sanctity.

Torah Centers and Educational Institutions

Beit Knesset Ahavat Chaim in Jerusalem: Located at 13 Chaim Ozer Street, it continues to serve as a grassroots Sephardic Torah center, where the prayer customs and tiqqunim founded by Hakham Menahem are preserved.

Beit Midrash for Halakhah Ahavat Chaim in Herzliya: An organization operating to train avrekhim for the rabbinate ("Yoreh Yoreh"), to provide instruction for grooms and brides, and to strengthen religious observance within the local community, all for the elevation of the soul of Hakham Menahem Manasseh.

Toledot Menahem Publications: His grandson, Rabbi Yosef Nehman Shabtai (the second), dedicated his life to preserving and disseminating his grandfather's Torah. He published new editions of "Ahavat Chaim," "Liqqutei Manasseh," and the pamphlet "Sha'ar HaChaim," alongside a comprehensive biography entitled "Toledot Menahem" documenting the lives of the hidden righteous in Jerusalem.

Summary of His Figure and Its Significance for Generations

Hakham Menahem Manasseh was a living bridge between worlds. He brought with him the depth and tranquility of Bursa and Istanbul into the noise and tumult of the renewing Jerusalem. His way in Torah was not elitist or detached; he wrote for the people, acted on behalf of the people, and labored for his sustenance together with the people.

His book "Ahavat Chaim" (Love of Life) remains a foundational work because it does not content itself with teaching dry law, but envelops it in the warmth of tales of the righteous and the consolation of aggadot of the Sages. He demonstrated that one could be a divine mequbbal while simultaneously being an impoverished tinsmith, that one could engage in cosmic tiqqunim at night and provide for the sustenance of orphans by day. The figure of Hakham Menahem Manasseh is a reminder that true sanctity is not found in separation from the public, but in absolute devotion to it, from a love that depends on nothing—ahavat chaim, love of life.
